title: Special-Purpose Frameworks
description: Understand financial statements prepared using cash basis, modified cash basis, tax basis and other special-purpose frameworks.
html:
What is a special-purpose framework?

Financial statements are often prepared under U.S. GAAP, but U.S. GAAP is not the only framework that may be used for financial reporting.

Certain entities may prepare financial statements using another appropriate financial reporting framework designed to meet a particular reporting purpose.

Common special-purpose frameworks

  • Cash basis
  • Tax basis
  • Regulatory basis
  • Contractual basis

CPA mindset

When you see special-purpose financial statements, first determine:

  1. What framework is being used?
  2. How does that framework recognize revenues, expenses, assets and liabilities?
  3. How does it differ from U.S. GAAP?
  4. What adjustments would be needed to convert from one basis to another?

Cash-basis accounting

Under a pure cash basis, revenues are generally recognized when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid.

This differs significantly from accrual accounting, which recognizes economic events without requiring the related cash movement to occur at the same time.

Cash Basis

Focuses primarily on cash receipts and payments.

Accrual Basis

Recognizes revenues and expenses according to the applicable recognition requirements, regardless of the timing of cash.

Cash versus accrual revenue

Example

A company performs $20,000 of services in December but will not collect the customer until January.

Cash basis

No December cash receipt occurred.

Accrual basis

Assuming the revenue-recognition requirements are satisfied, the company recognizes the revenue in December.

Converting cash-basis revenue to accrual-basis revenue

CPA questions may give you cash collections and changes in receivables and ask you to determine accrual-basis revenue.

Accrual Revenue = Cash Collected + Ending Accounts Receivable − Beginning Accounts Receivable

Cash collected from customers: $500,000

Beginning Accounts Receivable: $40,000

Ending Accounts Receivable: $65,000

$500,000 + $65,000 − $40,000 = $525,000

Accrual-basis revenue is $525,000.

Why the receivable adjustment works

If Accounts Receivable increases, the company recognized more revenue than it collected in cash.

Therefore, an increase in receivables is added to cash collections when converting to accrual-basis revenue.

  • A/R increases → add the increase
  • A/R decreases → subtract the decrease

Cash versus accrual expenses

Cash payments also do not necessarily equal accrual-basis expenses.

Accounts payable and prepaid expenses are common adjustments.

Accounts payable adjustment

Accrual Expense = Cash Paid + Ending Accounts Payable − Beginning Accounts Payable

Cash paid for operating expenses: $180,000

Beginning Accounts Payable: $25,000

Ending Accounts Payable: $37,000

$180,000 + $37,000 − $25,000 = $192,000

Accrual-basis expense is $192,000.

Reasoning

An increase in Accounts Payable means some expenses were recognized but have not yet been paid.

Therefore, those unpaid expenses must be added when converting cash payments to accrual expense.

Prepaid expense adjustment

Cash paid does not automatically become an expense immediately.

Some payments create assets because the related benefit applies to a future period.

Accrual Expense = Cash Paid + Beginning Prepaid Expense − Ending Prepaid Expense

Cash paid for insurance: $60,000

Beginning prepaid insurance: $8,000

Ending prepaid insurance: $14,000

$60,000 + $8,000 − $14,000 = $54,000

Accrual-basis insurance expense is $54,000.

Combined expense conversion

Some CPA problems combine payable and prepaid adjustments.

Accrual Expense = Cash Paid + Ending Payable − Beginning Payable + Beginning Prepaid − Ending Prepaid

Cash paid: $200,000

Accounts Payable increases: $15,000

Prepaid Expense increases: $6,000

$200,000 + $15,000 − $6,000 = $209,000

Accrual-basis expense is $209,000.

Tax-basis financial statements

Tax-basis financial statements generally use recognition and measurement concepts based on applicable income-tax rules rather than U.S. GAAP.

Because tax accounting and financial accounting can recognize items differently, tax-basis amounts may differ materially from U.S. GAAP amounts.

Differences can arise from

  • Revenue recognition
  • Depreciation
  • Expense deductibility
  • Capitalization requirements
  • Other tax-specific recognition and measurement rules

CPA trap

Tax-basis financial statements are not simply U.S. GAAP statements with income tax expense added.

The underlying measurement basis itself can differ.

Regulatory basis

Some entities operate in industries in which a regulatory authority prescribes a financial reporting framework for particular purposes.

Financial statements prepared according to such requirements may constitute regulatory-basis financial statements.

Contractual basis

Financial statements may also be prepared according to accounting requirements specified in a contractual agreement.

A lending agreement might define particular financial measurements or reporting requirements.

Statements prepared according to those contractual provisions may use a contractual basis of accounting.

Special-purpose does not mean incorrect

A financial statement prepared using a special-purpose framework is not automatically wrong merely because it differs from U.S. GAAP.

The key is identifying the framework being used and evaluating the statements according to that framework.

CPA trap

Do not assume:

Different from GAAP = Error

A legitimate special-purpose framework intentionally may produce different recognition or measurement.

Cash-to-accrual conversion framework

Accounts Receivable ↑ Revenue ↑
Accounts Receivable ↓ Revenue ↓
Accounts Payable ↑ Expense ↑
Accounts Payable ↓ Expense ↓
Prepaid Expense ↑ Expense ↓
Prepaid Expense ↓ Expense ↑

Worked CPA-style conversion

A cash-basis company reports $620,000 of customer cash receipts.

Accounts Receivable:

Beginning A/R $55,000
Ending A/R $82,000

Step 1 — Calculate the increase

$82,000 − $55,000 = $27,000 increase in A/R

Step 2 — Convert cash receipts to accrual revenue

$620,000 + $27,000 = $647,000

Accrual-basis revenue is $647,000.

What you should know after this lesson

  • Identify common special-purpose frameworks.
  • Distinguish cash-basis accounting from accrual accounting.
  • Convert cash collections into accrual-basis revenue.
  • Convert cash payments into accrual-basis expenses.
  • Correctly analyze Accounts Receivable, Accounts Payable and prepaid accounts.
  • Understand the general purpose of tax-basis financial statements.
  • Recognize regulatory and contractual frameworks.
  • Understand that a legitimate non-GAAP framework is not automatically an accounting error.

quiz.prompt: A company using the cash basis collected $750,000 from customers during the year. Accounts Receivable was $60,000 at the beginning of the year and $95,000 at year-end. What amount of revenue would generally be recognized when converting these amounts to the accrual basis?
quiz.explanation: Accounts Receivable increased by $35,000 ($95,000 − $60,000). This means accrual-basis revenue exceeded customer cash collections by $35,000. Therefore, accrual-basis revenue is $750,000 + $35,000 = $785,000.
